subject: Chemistry
description: Gas laws — Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, Avogadro's, ideal gas equation; STP conditions, real-world gas behaviour.

questions.stem: Boyle's Law states that at constant TEMPERATURE, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is:
questions.explanation: BOYLE'S LAW (Robert Boyle, 1662): at constant TEMPERATURE for a fixed mass of gas, P × V = constant, i.e., V ∝ 1/P. EXAMPLE: double the pressure → halve the volume; halve the pressure → double the volume. KEY GRAPH: P vs V is a hyperbola; PV vs P is a horizontal line; P vs 1/V is a straight line through origin. INTUITION: pushing gas molecules into smaller volume increases their wall-collision frequency → higher pressure. APPLICATIONS: (1) DEEP-SEA DIVING — at 30 m depth (4 atm pressure), lung gas volumes shrink to 1/4. (2) BICYCLE PUMP — compressing air heats it (the heat is from pressure work, not from Boyle alone). (3) HIGH-ALTITUDE BREATHING — at Mt Everest summit (~33% sea-level pressure), each breath carries only 1/3 the O₂ molecules. PYQ FREQUENCY: top-3 chemistry MCQ in NEET, JEE-Main, SSC; appears as a 1-mark guarantee. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests P-V relationship core fundamental.

questions.stem: Charles's Law states that at constant PRESSURE, the volume of a gas is:
questions.explanation: CHARLES'S LAW (Jacques Charles, 1787): at constant PRESSURE, V ∝ T (T in KELVIN). So V/T = constant; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. CRITICAL: T must be in KELVIN, NOT Celsius. K = °C + 273. EXAMPLE: gas at 27°C (300 K) → heated to 327°C (600 K) at constant P → volume DOUBLES. ABSOLUTE ZERO — graphical extrapolation: V vs T graph hits zero volume at −273.15°C — this defines absolute zero (0 K). HOT-AIR BALLOONS: warm air expands → less dense than surrounding cold air → BUOYANT lift. Above ~120°C the fabric softens; pilots vary altitude by adjusting burner heat. RUNNING SHOES: the air pockets in your soles compress in cold weather (Charles's law in reverse) — feel firmer. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 Charles-law numericals per JEE-Main, NEET. EXAM TRAP: students forget to convert °C to K and get wrong answers. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests T-V proportion + Kelvin discipline.

questions.stem: What is the IDEAL GAS EQUATION?

options.option_text: P + V = nRT alone alone (option here)

questions.explanation: IDEAL GAS EQUATION: PV = nRT, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = universal gas constant = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), T = temperature in Kelvin. ALTERNATE FORMS: PV = (m/M)RT (m = mass, M = molar mass); PV = NkT (N = molecules, k = Boltzmann constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K). COMBINATION OF GAS LAWS: ideal gas equation REPLACES Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws — they're special cases when the other variables are held constant. AT STP (Standard Temp & Pressure: 0°C / 273.15 K, 1 atm): 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 LITRES. NTP (Normal Temp & Pressure, 20°C, 1 atm): 1 mole = ~24.0 L. ASSUMPTIONS — IDEAL GAS: (1) Gas particles are point masses (no volume). (2) No intermolecular forces. (3) Collisions are perfectly elastic. REAL GASES deviate at HIGH P and LOW T — corrections via VAN DER WAALS equation. PYQ ANGLE: ideal gas is a top JEE-Main, NEET MCQ — 2-3 per paper.

questions.stem: Avogadro's Law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain:
questions.explanation: AVOGADRO'S LAW (Amedeo Avogadro, 1811): equal volumes of gases at same T and P contain EQUAL numbers of MOLECULES (NOT equal mass — molecular weights differ). MATHEMATICALLY: V ∝ n (at constant T, P). AVOGADRO'S NUMBER: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mole — defines the mole, the SI unit of substance. AT STP: 1 mole = 22.4 L = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. APPLICATION: this law IS what allows chemical equations to be balanced in terms of MOLAR ratios → VOLUME ratios for gases. EXAMPLE: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — 2 volumes hydrogen + 1 volume oxygen → 2 volumes water vapour. NOBEL: Avogadro's hypothesis was ignored for ~50 years; Cannizzaro revived it (1860). MOLE CONCEPT in NCERT Class 11 Ch. 1 — foundational. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'mole/Avogadro' is a 1-mark guarantee in JEE-Main, NEET, SSC; appears 1-2× per CGL Tier 1 paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests molecular-vs-mass distinction, often a student-confusion source.

questions.stem: At STP (0°C, 1 atm), what volume does 1 mole of any ideal gas occupy?
questions.explanation: AT STP (Standard Temperature & Pressure: 273.15 K and 1 atm = 101.325 kPa): 1 mole of any ideal gas = 22.4 L = 22,400 cm³ = 22,400 mL. DERIVATION: V = nRT/P = 1 × 0.0821 × 273.15 / 1 ≈ 22.4 L. NOTE: IUPAC redefined STP in 1982 to 0°C and 100 kPa (~24 L for 1 mole) — but the CLASSIC 22.4 L is still the textbook standard for SSC, NEET, JEE-Main. APPLICATION — molar mass via gas density: M = (mass)(22.4) / (volume in L at STP). EXAMPLE: 22 g of CO₂ occupies (22/44) × 22.4 = 11.2 L at STP. PRACTICE — 11.2 L of any gas at STP = 0.5 mole = ~3 × 10²³ molecules. NTP variant: 20°C, 1 atm → 1 mole ~24.0 L. PYQ FREQUENCY: '22.4 L at STP' is a 1-mark MCQ in 90% of JEE-Main, NEET papers. SSC and CGL include this in the chemistry segment 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests STP molar volume — a fundamental gas-stoichiometry skill.

questions.stem: A gas at 27°C is heated to 127°C at constant pressure. What is the ratio of final to initial volume?
questions.explanation: Apply CHARLES'S LAW: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. CONVERT to KELVIN: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K. So V₂/V₁ = T₂/T₁ = 400/300 = 4/3. INSIGHT: even though Celsius temperature changed by 100° (a big-feeling jump), in Kelvin the change is only from 300 to 400 K — a 33% increase. EXAM TRAP: students wrongly compute V₂/V₁ = 127/27 ≈ 4.7 (using °C directly) — gives a totally wrong answer. ALWAYS USE KELVIN for gas-law calculations. WHY KELVIN? Because Kelvin is an ABSOLUTE scale (0 K = no molecular motion), while Celsius has an arbitrary zero (water's freezing point). Gas-law ratios only make sense at absolute zero reference. PYQ FREQUENCY: this exact 27°C/127°C pair appears in JEE-Main, NEET 2-3× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests °C-to-K conversion + Charles's law application + ratio simplification.

questions.stem: Real gases deviate from ideal-gas behaviour MOST under conditions of:
questions.explanation: Real gases deviate from PV = nRT MOST at LOW T and HIGH P. WHY? At LOW T: kinetic energy is low → INTERMOLECULAR ATTRACTIONS become significant (attractive forces ignored in ideal-gas model). At HIGH P: gas molecules are pushed close together → MOLECULAR VOLUME becomes significant compared to container volume (ideal-gas model assumes point particles). Both deviations correct via VAN DER WAALS EQUATION: (P + a·n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT — where 'a' corrects for attraction, 'b' for molecular volume. CRITICAL POINT: above the critical temperature, a gas can't be liquefied no matter the pressure; below, it can be. EXAMPLES — gases LIQUEFY at low T, high P: O₂, N₂, CO₂, He (extreme). REAL-WORLD: liquid nitrogen (storage of biological samples, MRI cooling) — produced via Linde process (compression-expansion cycles). PYQ ANGLE: deviation conditions appear in JEE-Main 1× per year, NEET 1× per year. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests grasp of WHY ideal-gas model breaks down — concept beyond rote.
